newsitem.title: USA: University of California mulls new diversity plan.
newsitem.headline: University of California mulls new diversity plan.

text.p: A University of California task force Tuesday recommended the school expand outreach to disadvantaged students and change its admissions process to assure the continuation of a diverse student body.
The plan was proposed to make up for diversity lost as a result of the university system's July 1995 decision to eliminate the use of race, ethnicity and gender in the admissions process.
Under the new plan, the university would work closely with a group of elementary and secondary schools identifed as ones where students were at a significant educational disadvantage.
"We're trying to qualify more minority students for admission, rather than accepting them on the basis of affirmative action," said a spokesman for the university.

C. Judson King, U.C. provost and senior vice president for academic affairs, said that despite a 30-year tradition of outreach efforts, "a gap clearly continues to exist between the very high standards of achievement required for U.C. admission and the uneven record of students from different socioeconomic, ethnic, racial and geographic backgrounds."

"We believe this plan will narrow that gap significantly and make outreach the university's primary tool for recruiting a diverse student body," added King, who served as a co-chair of the task force.

Last week, the University of California at Berkeley's Boalt Hall law school reported a sharp drop in minority admissions in its first class without affirmative action. The number of African American students admitted for this fall's entering class fell to 14 from 75 last year, and Hispanic and Puerto Rican student admissions dropped to 16 from 34.

Under the plan unveiled Tuesday, the university would consider mitigating factors such as socioeconomic status or attendance in secondary schools with poor college-preparatory courses, rather than race, ethnicity and gender.

The official admission standard for the University of California system is for students to rank in the top 12.5 percent of students in the state, based on grades and test scores. But because students from different races fall unevenly into that group, the school has traditionally based a portion of its admissions on other factors.

About 12.7 percent of the state's white high school seniors meet the school's academic admission standards, compared with five percent of the hispanics, 3.5 percent of African American students and 38 percent of Asian students.

The proposed diversity plan is open to public comment before the university decides whether to adopt it. The U.C. system has nine campuses and 127,000 undergraduate students, along with 167,000 graduate students.
